strengths: The paper identifies a practically important failure mode: current VLMs often substitute familiar object knowledge for fine-grained visual evidence.
VLMBias is broad, containing 1,392 counterfactual images across seven domains, multiple resolutions, two prompt paraphrases, and five recent proprietary VLMs.

The systematic one-element modifications and bias-aligned error analysis are intuitive and yield striking empirical patterns; the in-image text and prompting interventions add useful diagnostic evidence.
The appendix provides extensive task-generation details, prompts, model identifiers, and qualitative examples.
weaknesses: The central causal claim that failures are caused by prior-knowledge bias is not adequately isolated from ordinary visual-resolution, attention, and counting limitations. The paper lacks matched controls using equally sized and complex but unfamiliar objects, decontextualized crops, or noncanonical objects without strong semantic priors. This is especially serious because some targets, such as car logos, are extremely small and the paper itself notes a fundamental counting inability.

The sanity check is not a sufficient control: only 66 unmodified images are used, rather than matched originals for every counterfactual instance, and many questions can be answered correctly from world knowledge without inspecting the image. Thus, 100% performance does not establish that models can visually resolve and count the relevant elements under matched conditions.

There is no human-performance or annotation-agreement study. Manual filtering by the authors alone cannot establish that generated extra limbs and logos are unambiguous or that modified illusion differences are perceptually evident at each resolution.

Several binary ground truths are semantically questionable. A four-stripe Adidas-style mark may still be identifiable as an Adidas logo, a slightly altered flag may still depict a country's flag, and an Ebbinghaus configuration can remain an example of that illusion even when its central circles differ. Treating every modified instance as an unequivocal 'No' weakens the Q3 results.

Reported observations are highly correlated: the same base image is reused at three resolutions and with two near-equivalent prompts, yet results are presented without confidence intervals, statistical tests, per-base-image aggregation, or analysis of run-to-run variation. Each temperature-1 model query also appears to be sampled only once.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a benchmark paper relying on changing proprietary APIs: access dates and several generation details are missing, the manuscript's code/data URL is blank, and evaluation uses default settings without fully documenting all decoding and image-processing parameters.

The work is primarily diagnostic and overlaps substantially with prior counterfactual hallucination and visual-shortcoming benchmarks. Its broader taxonomy and scale are useful, but without stronger controls the evidence does not support the paper's stronger novelty and bias-attribution claims.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important and easily understood failure mode: VLMs often answer according to familiar visual templates instead of small counterfactual changes.
The benchmark spans seven domains and evaluates five strong proprietary VLMs, including reasoning and non-reasoning models.

The authors provide systematic generation procedures, multiple resolutions, prompt variants, and useful qualitative examples. The planned release of data and generation/evaluation code could benefit diagnostic research.
The very high rate of prior-aligned responses is an interesting empirical observation, even if its proposed causal interpretation is not established.
weaknesses: The central attribution to memorized bias is not isolated from basic visual limitations. The modifications are deliberately subtle, logos can be extremely small, and the tasks require difficult counting or localization. There are no matched unfamiliar-symbol, cropped/zoomed, equal-salience, or otherwise bias-free controls. The patterned-grid results actually demonstrate that similar failures occur without Internet memorization.

The original-image sanity check is inadequate: only 66 unmodified images are tested, versus 1,392 reported counterfactual images, and these are not clearly paired item-by-item with the counterfactual conditions. Recognizing an ordinary animal or flag does not establish that an added limb or symbol is perceptually clear.

No human study quantifies whether the counterfactual details and ground-truth answers are reliably visible. Images are manually selected after generation, but the number and qualifications of reviewers, annotation protocol, agreement, rejection rate, and ambiguity resolution are missing.

Several Q3 labels are semantically invalid. A flag with one altered star can still be recognized as the flag of its country; an altered Adidas-style mark may still be called an Adidas logo; and changing target measurements does not necessarily mean an image is no longer an example of an Ebbinghaus or Müller-Lyer illusion. Treating every modified image as having the answer “No” undermines the reported 25.11% identification accuracy.

The statistical evaluation is weak. Three resolutions of the same underlying image and two near-identical question paraphrases are treated as many observations, yet no confidence intervals, clustered analysis, significance tests, or per-resolution results are provided. Models are sampled at temperature 1.0 apparently only once, so stochastic variability is unknown.

The in-image-text experiment is also confounded: adding a title extends the canvas and can change the effective scale after API preprocessing. Consequently, the accuracy drop cannot be attributed solely to textual bias without a matched irrelevant-text control and scale-preserving construction.

Reproducibility is incomplete for API models: evaluation dates, fully immutable model versions, decoding/output-parsing details, failure handling, seeds, and repeated trials are absent. “Default settings” are neither stable nor necessarily comparable across providers.

The manuscript is unfinished in a material way: Appendix L.5 introduces an error-distribution analysis on page 48, but page 49 contains only the continuation of its introductory paragraph and reports no method or results.

The novelty and positioning are limited relative to existing counterfactual hallucination, language-prior, optical-illusion, and low-level visual-counting benchmarks. The broader task coverage is useful, but the evidence does not support the stronger claim that these failures are primarily caused by memorized textual knowledge.

strengths: Introduces a timely and practically relevant benchmark for testing whether VLMs prioritize learned expectations over contradictory visual evidence.

The empirical pattern is striking and consistent: across five strong proprietary VLMs and seven domains, mean counterfactual counting accuracy is only 17.05%, while 75.70% of predictions are bias-aligned.
The evaluation covers diverse photorealistic and programmatically generated settings, including animals, logos, flags, board games, optical illusions, and novel patterned grids.
Bias-aligned errors, paired original/counterfactual conditions, in-image textual cues, two prompt variants, and three image resolutions provide multiple complementary views of the failure mode.
The automated generation pipelines, manual quality filtering, detailed prompts, model versions, and promised release of data and code support reproducibility and future benchmarking.
The paper is clearly motivated, accessible, and supported by effective qualitative examples and extensive per-domain results.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation is not fully isolated from generic fine-grained perception and counting failures. Several targets, especially car logos and large grids, are extremely small; matched unfamiliar controls, cropped or zoomed inputs, and equally difficult non-counterfactual counting tasks are needed to distinguish prior-induced bias from simple visual-resolution limitations.

The unmodified-image sanity check is insufficient for this distinction: recognizing an object and returning its conventional count can itself be accomplished from prior knowledge, without perceiving the relevant elements. It also uses only 66 images rather than a fully paired control for every counterfactual sample.
No human-performance study or quantified annotation agreement is reported. Manual filtering alone does not establish that every edited image is unambiguous at each tested resolution.

The nominal 1,392 images include three resized copies of each underlying scene, and Q1/Q2 are close paraphrases. Results therefore contain substantial dependence, yet the paper provides no confidence intervals, significance tests, hierarchical analysis, or reporting by resolution.

Models are sampled with temperature 1 using apparently one response per condition. Repeated runs are needed to quantify stochastic variability, particularly when reported differences between interventions or model classes are only a few percentage points.

Some Q3 ground-truth labels are conceptually questionable: a recognizable Adidas-, Audi-, or national-flag design does not necessarily cease being that identity merely because one graphical element was modified. These results should be framed as conformity judgments or excluded from the strongest claims.

The benchmark evaluates only proprietary API models and provides limited inference details beyond default settings. Including reproducible open-weight VLMs, text-only and image-only controls, crop/zoom baselines, and stronger comparison benchmarks would substantially improve diagnostic value.

The broad claim that these failures demonstrate memorized Internet knowledge is stronger than the evidence for every task. The novel patterned-grid results instead reflect global-context priors, and the paper should more carefully separate semantic knowledge bias, contextual expectation, and basic visual limitations.

strengths: The paper identifies an important and practically relevant failure mode: VLMs often substitute canonical knowledge for contradictory visual evidence, even under neutral counting prompts.
VLMBias is broad and systematic, covering 1,392 counterfactual images across seven domains, multiple resolutions, two prompt variants, and both photographic and programmatically generated images.

The evaluation is unusually extensive: commercial and open-source models, repeated trials, human comparisons, prompting interventions, background removal, tool use, pointing-capable models, and vision-encoder probing all provide useful complementary evidence.

The central descriptive result is compelling and consistent: accuracy is low across model families, while incorrect responses frequently equal a predefined canonical answer. The patterned-grid task usefully demonstrates that the phenomenon also occurs with within-image regularities rather than only memorized world knowledge.
The paper is clearly organized, provides prompts and model settings, and includes many qualitative examples that make the observed behavior easy to understand.
weaknesses: Several causal conclusions are stronger than the experiments support. A linear probe showing that pooled encoder features predict leg count does not establish that the language model “overrides” visual evidence; the failure could arise in the projector, token bottleneck, attention, spatial binding, or decoding process.

The background-removal intervention is substantially confounded. It uses segmentation or cropping for photographs but regenerated SVGs or modified scripts for abstract images, simultaneously changing object scale, salience, composition, and visual distribution. The reported gain therefore cannot be attributed specifically to background cues.

The claim that overthinking harms accuracy is based on observational binning of adaptively chosen reasoning lengths. Item difficulty and model confidence affect how many tokens are used, so the curve does not establish that additional reasoning causes lower accuracy. A controlled reasoning-budget experiment is needed.

Human validation covers only the animal subset, although ambiguity and annotation validity are at least as concerning for logos and optical illusions. For example, whether a modified Adidas-like mark remains an “Adidas logo,” or whether a modified display remains an example of an illusion, is semantically debatable. Manual filtering lacks reported annotator counts, agreement, and acceptance criteria.

The effective diversity is smaller than the stated image count suggests: three resolutions and two near-paraphrased questions repeat the same underlying scenes. Results lack uncertainty estimates or paired statistical tests and do not clearly account for this dependence.

Some secondary conclusions are under-supported, including inverse scaling, “more knowledge leads to more bias,” and overconfidence causing low tool use. Comparisons involve few non-equivalent models and provide correlations rather than controlled evidence.

There are reporting inconsistencies, such as Table 14 describing a +1.9-point tool improvement while the accompanying text reports +4.83 using a different baseline, and Table 16's caption mistakenly comparing 36.02% against 36.02% for commercial models. These issues should be corrected and all aggregation conventions clarified.

The ethical reporting for the human study is incomplete: consent and minimal risk are mentioned, but recruitment, compensation, institutional review status or exemption, and exclusion criteria are not documented.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant VLM failure mode: familiar semantic context can coincide with poor recognition of counterfactual visual details.
The evaluation is broad, covering seven domains and numerous commercial, open-weight, reasoning, and pointing-capable VLMs.

The benchmark uses neutral counting prompts, multiple resolutions, two prompt formulations, repeated-run checks for two models, and several useful interventions such as cropping, in-image text, prompting, and tool use.
The comparison with specialized pointing models is informative and suggests a promising direction for improving visually grounded counting.
The appendix provides extensive prompts, model identifiers, generation procedures, examples, and disaggregated results.
weaknesses: The central causal conclusion—that language-model priors override adequately encoded visual evidence—is not established by the design. Canonical and counterfactual conditions are confounded with image editing or regeneration, visual difficulty, target size, occlusion, and possible generation artifacts. Perfect performance on easier canonical images does not isolate prior-knowledge bias.

The background-removal experiment is not a controlled background intervention. It also changes cropping, object scale, clutter, and sometimes the underlying rendering through regenerated SVGs or scripts. Consequently, the reported gain cannot be attributed specifically to background bias.

The linear probe does not demonstrate that the encoder counts legs or that the language model suppresses this information. A classifier may exploit generator artifacts or other class-correlated features; the paper reports no cross-generator, species-disjoint, or artifact-controlled split. Moreover, this experiment concerns one SigLIP/LLaVA configuration but is generalized to unrelated proprietary VLMs.

Dataset validity is insufficiently established. Authors manually select generated counterfactuals without reporting independent annotations, inter-annotator agreement, rejection rates, or systematic ground-truth verification. The human study covers only the animal subset, uses multiple-choice answers rather than the VLM protocol, and therefore does not validate the other six domains.

Several evaluations contain answer and construction confounds. For Q3, original examples always have the answer Yes and counterfactual examples No, so the result mixes counterfactual sensitivity with response preference. Some identity questions, such as whether a modified logo remains an Adidas logo, are semantically debatable. The optical-illusion task also differs substantially from the counting tasks yet is included in aggregate means.

The reasoning-length analysis is observational rather than an intervention on test-time compute. Question difficulty and model confidence jointly determine reasoning length, bins have highly unequal support (occasionally n=1), and no uncertainty estimates are supplied. Thus the claimed rise followed by harm from overthinking is not justified.

The inverse-scaling and 'more knowledge leads to more bias' claims are based on only two architecture-confounded model pairs. Parameter count, training data, vision encoders, instruction tuning, and inference systems all differ, preventing the proposed interpretation.

Most headline results appear to use a single stochastic run at temperature 1.0; five-run analysis is limited to two models. The three resolutions are transformations of the same underlying examples and should not be treated as independent evidence. Statistical uncertainty or paired significance tests are generally absent.

There are internal reporting inconsistencies: the tool-use discussion alternately describes the improvement as +1.9 and +4.83 because it compares different baselines, and it similarly reports incompatible bias-rate changes. Table 16's caption also states a comparison of 36.02% versus 36.02%. These errors reduce confidence in the quantitative presentation.

Overall, the benchmark may be useful descriptively, but the paper repeatedly turns correlations and heavily confounded interventions into strong mechanistic claims. Addressing those issues would require matched image controls, independent dataset validation, experimentally controlled reasoning budgets, and substantially more careful statistical analysis.

The empirical coverage is unusually broad: seven domains, five principal commercial VLMs, additional recent and open models, and comparisons with pointing-specialized models. The large performance drops and high rates of canonical answers are striking and consistent across model families.

The paper includes many useful controls and analyses, including unmodified images, identification questions, background removal, in-image text, debiasing and double-check prompts, repeated trials, resolution analysis, few-shot prompting, tool use, human evaluation, and vision-encoder probing.

The findings concerning pointing models and tool underutilization are actionable: they suggest that explicit localization/counting mechanisms can help substantially, while general models often fail to invoke available visual tools.

The appendix documents model identifiers, prompts, generation procedures, and task-specific ground-truth rules in considerable detail; the promised release of code and data would make the benchmark a useful community resource.
The paper is clearly motivated and visually well presented, with informative examples that make the failure mode easy to understand.
weaknesses: The central causal interpretation—that language-model priors override available visual evidence—is not fully isolated. Canonical answers can arise from generic failures of attention, localization, or counting rather than memorized knowledge specifically. The unmodified-image sanity check is weak evidence because models can answer those images correctly using the same canonical priors without inspecting the relevant visual elements.

The background-removal intervention is substantially confounded: segmentation or reconstruction changes target size, salience, clutter, composition, and sometimes the rendering process itself. Thus, the reported gain does not cleanly establish that semantic background cues trigger bias. Matched controls that alter salience without removing semantic context, and vice versa, are needed.

The linear probe shows that information distinguishing four- from five-legged generated mammals is decodable from one open model's frozen encoder, but it does not demonstrate actual leg counting or a causal override by the language decoder. It uses a different model from the main evaluation, a binary generated dataset that may contain editing artifacts, and average-pooled features; stronger causal interventions or localization probes would be more convincing.

The headline aggregate mixes heterogeneous tasks and chance levels: optical-illusion binary questions are combined with open-ended counting, while tasks are macro-averaged equally. Moreover, the stated 1,392 images include three resized copies of each of roughly 464 underlying scenes, and Q1/Q2 are near-duplicate prompts. The paper should distinguish unique semantic examples from rendered queries and provide per-example clustered uncertainty.

Claims of statistically significant differences are made without confidence intervals or hypothesis tests. Five-run variability is reported only for two models, and the paper lacks uncertainty estimates for most comparisons, including background removal, model-family differences, and apparent inverse scaling.

Human validation covers only the animal task, while image quality and unambiguity in the other generated or modified domains rely mainly on unspecified manual review. The number of reviewers, rejection rates, annotation protocol, and inter-rater agreement are not reported, leaving possible benchmark artifacts insufficiently quantified.

Several presentation inconsistencies need correction, including conflicting descriptions of the tool-enabled improvement (+1.9 on the matched high-resolution subset versus +4.83 against the overall baseline) and the erroneous Table 16 caption comparing 36.02% with 36.02%. These do not overturn the main phenomenon but reduce confidence in the quantitative reporting.
